Oral and maxillofacial surgery · published research

Palatal donor-site wound healing

PBM may improve selected early healing measures after graft harvesting, but effects on overall wound closure, pain, and analgesic use are not consistent.

Summary of the Evidence

PBM may improve early epithelialization or reduce palatal wound area after gingival graft harvesting. The clinical evidence is small and mixed: some trials report faster wound healing, while a later dual-wavelength trial found no significant overall improvement in wound closure, pain, or analgesic use.

Human and clinical evidence

The exact PBM Database category contains ten unique titles: four randomized clinical reports and six animal publications. One mouse publication also carries an in-vitro tag; it is a component of that same paper, not an eleventh title or an additional clinical cohort.

In a 36-person randomized trial after free gingival graft harvesting, PBM and injectable platelet-rich fibrin (i-PRF) were compared with control. Wound areas were larger in controls than in both active-treatment groups at selected follow-up days. Pain was higher in controls on days 3 and 14, while analgesia use favored PBM over control on day 3. The trial did not establish that PBM was superior to i-PRF (Bozkurt and Özdemir 2025).

A 2022 split-mouth sham-controlled trial with 14 completers found smaller remaining wound areas with PBM at days 7 and 14, but no significant pain or discomfort difference (Morshedzadeh et al. 2022).

Earlier dose-comparison studies also reported smaller wounds or faster healing at selected time points. Dias et al. found smaller wounds at days 14 and 45 after a 660-nm protocol; da Silva Neves et al. concluded that 60 J/cm² produced faster wound-area reduction at day 7 than the lower-dose regimen. A 2016 study of 30 patients measured growth factors and cytokines in wound fluid, which are surrogate rather than patient-important outcomes (Dias et al. 2015; da Silva Neves et al. 2016; Keskiner et al. 2016).

A 2025 randomized trial of 30 patients after de-epithelialized graft harvesting found no significant overall difference in wound closure, pain, or analgesic use with dual-wavelength PBM, although more treated wounds had complete epithelial coverage by day 10 (Paz et al. 2025).

A 2026 PBM-specific systematic review included eight RCTs and 284 participants. Most studies favored early epithelialization, wound-area reduction, or tissue color, but the review reported no pooled effect estimate and its search ended on April 7, 2025, before the two relevant trials published later that year (Araújo et al. 2026). A broader 2021 meta-analysis of 13 periodontal-surgery trials found less pain at day 3 but not day 7, reduced analgesic intake during the first week, and faster palatal re-epithelialization at day 14. Its findings support a possible early effect but are not specific to every palatal graft protocol (Zhao et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

Six animal publications are indexed: three rat and three mouse studies. These models investigate palatal mucosal repair and inflammatory or cellular responses but cannot determine patient-important benefits after graft harvesting.

In-vitro component

One in-vitro tag overlaps a mouse study of gingival mesenchymal stem-cell migration and wound healing. It remains part of that publication and is not an additional clinical study (Feng et al. 2020).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols vary. Indexed examples include 660-nm PBM at 3 J/cm² over eight sessions, a 30-versus-60-J/cm² comparison, 1064 nm at 1.6 J/cm² for wound-fluid biomarkers, and a 980-nm five-session protocol. The database does not provide complete fluence and exposure details for every trial. The later dual-wavelength trial used five applications from surgery through postoperative day 15, but its abstract does not state the wavelengths or dose. No optimal regimen can be inferred from these studies.

Interpretation

Evidence supports a possible improvement in selected early healing measures, especially epithelialization and wound area. Confidence is low because trials are small, wound measures and comparators differ, and pain or overall-closure benefits are inconsistent. Evidence is very uncertain for superiority over active dressings or platelet products and for lasting tissue quality. Larger trials should use blinded wound measurement, report complete laser parameters, compare PBM with usual care and active interventions, and follow epithelialization, pain, analgesic use, scarring, and tissue quality beyond the first weeks.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Broader periodontal-surgery synthesis — pain favored PBM at day 3 but not day 7; analgesic intake was lower during week one; palatal re-epithelialization was faster at day 14 (Zhao et al. 2021).

Palatal donor-site trials — selected studies report smaller wounds or faster epithelialization. A 2022 sham-controlled trial found a smaller wound area but no pain difference; a 30-person 2025 trial found no significant overall closure, pain, or analgesic-use difference (Morshedzadeh et al. 2022; Bozkurt and Özdemir 2025; Paz et al. 2025).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for early wound-area reduction or re-epithelialization versus usual care. Very low for superiority over active dressings or platelet products and for durable tissue quality.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The 2026 review included eight RCTs but reported no pooled effect estimate; its search predates two relevant 2025 trials. In one small trial, PBM and i-PRF both performed better than control on selected outcomes without establishing a difference between the active treatments. Another small trial found earlier epithelialization but no significant overall closure, pain, or analgesic benefit. Protocols, wound measurements, co-interventions, and follow-up differ, and long-term tissue quality is sparsely assessed.
